title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
hookLine: after the huge catch, Peter falls down: I'm a sinful man; Jesus says fear not

lines: A NIGHT SHIFT WITH NOTHING TO SHOW.
cards: Simon has been up all night with nothing to show for it: sore arms, cold hands, empty nets. He and his partners are on the shore, washing their nets, the last chore before sleep.
A crowd is pressing in on a teacher by the water, so close he steps into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little. Jesus sits and teaches from the boat.
Then he turns to the tired fisherman and says something no fisherman wants to hear at the end of a bad night: let's go out again.

teach.h: WE HAVE TOILED ALL THE NIGHT.
teach.b: "Launch out into the deep, and let down your nets for a draught."
Simon's answer, in the King James words, is tired and honest at once: "Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing: nevertheless at thy word I will let down the net." Nevertheless.
That one word holds his exhaustion and his trust. The nets fill so full they start to tear. They wave to their partners in the other boat, and both boats fill until they begin to sink.

teach.h: DEPART FROM ME; I AM A SINFUL MAN.
teach.b: Instead, "he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord." Go away from me. In Luke's telling, Simon looks at what just happened, then at himself, and wants distance.

People still do something like it: when kindness comes unexpectedly, some of us deflect, or joke, or say you shouldn't have. Jesus doesn't argue about whether Simon is a sinner. He doesn't go away either.
He says: "Fear not; from henceforth thou shalt catch men."

teach.h: FEAR NOT; FROM HENCEFORTH THOU SHALT CATCH MEN.
teach.b: Luke's Greek word for catch here is zogreo, which lexicons give as to take alive. Not fish for the market: catching to keep alive, the way you pull someone out of the water.
And Luke ends: "they forsook all, and followed him." Two boats full of fish, left on the beach.

how: Christians read the great catch of fish as the call of the first disciples, and some churches use "launch out into the deep" to encourage people to begin something new in faith.

o: to haul in a full net of fish for market
to cast a net out into the deep water
to catch alive, as you'd pull someone from water

games.q: you're Simon. the nets are tearing, the boats are sinking, and you're looking at the man who told you where to fish. what do you do?
o: haul in the fish and start counting.
fall at his knees: depart from me, I'm a sinful man.
ask him to come fishing every night.
games.why: Simon falls down and asks him to go away. Jesus doesn't leave. he says: fear not.

practice: Think of a kindness you pushed away: a compliment you argued with, a gift you said was too much, help you refused because you didn't want to owe anyone.
Notice the small voice that says depart from me, I don't deserve this, then picture that kindness coming again and let it land.
If you pray, you can hear Jesus' answer to Simon as if it were spoken to you, fear not; if you don't, simply let the kindness stay.

wordCard.voice: Zogreo, Luke's Greek word for catching alive: Simon's cry after the great catch, overwhelmed by goodness, and the answer he gets instead, fear not.

orig.note: Greek: catching alive. "thou shalt catch men": to take alive, to rescue.

carryVoice: Your line: fear not. Goodness doesn't have to be pushed away, even when it surprises you. See you tomorrow.
